Solution
Words: 61
a OurBigBook.com
A complex derivative computed along the real and imaginary directions gives f′=ux​+ivx​=vy​−iuy​. Equality yields the Cauchy-Riemann equations
ux​=vy​,uy​=−vx​.​
(1)
The gradients satisfy ∇u⋅∇v=ux​vx​+uy​vy​=0. Since a gradient is normal to a regular level set, the two families meet at right angles by orthogonality wherever f′=0. At a critical point the regular-curve argument fails: for f=z2 both gradients vanish at zero, so the assertion requires this qualification.

b

Words: 56 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 56
b OurBigBook.com
Set A=x2−y2 and B=2xy. Direct differentiation gives
uxx​=e−B[(4y2−4x2)sinA+(2−8xy)cosA],uyy​=e−B[(4x2−4y2)sinA+(8xy−2)cosA].
(2)
Their sum vanishes, proving that u is a harmonic function. More generally the Cauchy-Riemann equations give uxx​+uyy​=vyx​−vxy​=0 and vxx​+vyy​=−uyx​+uxy​=0; the mixed partial derivatives commute because a holomorphic function is smooth. Since eiz2=e−B(cosA+isinA), a harmonic conjugate and the resulting holomorphic function are
v=−e−2xycos(x2−y2)+C,f(z)=−ieiz2+iC,C∈R.​
(3)
These expressions also verify the Cauchy-Riemann equations directly.

The chain rule in polar coordinates gives ur​=ux​cosθ+uy​sinθ and uθ​=r(−ux​sinθ+uy​cosθ), with analogous expressions for v. Substituting the Cauchy-Riemann equations gives
rur​=vθ​,rvr​=−uθ​,r>0.​
(4)
The restriction excludes the coordinate singularity at the origin.

Choose a continuous branch of a multivalued function of the complex logarithm on a simply connected region avoiding zero. Then
g=e−θeilnr=eiLogz,g′(z)=zi​g(z).​
(5)
Alternatively ur​=−e−θsin(lnr)/r=vθ​/r and vr​=e−θcos(lnr)/r=−uθ​/r, verifying the Cauchy-Riemann equations. The holomorphy is local to a chosen branch of a multivalued function: increasing θ by 2π multiplies g by e−2π, so this is not a single-valued holomorphic function on the whole punctured plane.

For n≥1, f=znen/z is holomorphic at every finite nonzero point. At zero its Laurent series has infinitely many negative powers, so zero is an essential singularity. If the Riemann sphere is included, f(1/w)=w−nenw has a pole of order n at w=0, so infinity is a pole of order n.

Solution
Words: 51
a OurBigBook.com
Cauchy's integral theorem states that a holomorphic function on a simply connected open region has zero contour integral around every closed piecewise smooth contour in that region. More generally the same holds for a contour homologous to zero in its domain of holomorphy. Having no singularity on the curve alone is insufficient: 1/z has a nonzero contour integral around the unit circle.

Put z=eiθ, so dθ=dz/(iz), cos2θ=(z2+z−2)/2 and cos23θ=(z6+2+z−6)/4. The contour integral is
4i1​∮∣z∣=1​z(5z2−2z4−2)z8+2z2+z−4​dz.
(9)
The enclosed poles are 0 and ±1/2​. For the rational function displayed without the prefactor 1/(4i), the residue at zero is −21/8 and the two other residues sum to 27/8. Therefore the residue theorem gives
∫02π​5−4cos2θcos23θ​dθ=4i1​(2πi)43​=83π​.​
(10)
A useful independent check is the Fourier series (5−4cosϕ)−1=31​[1+2∑k≥1​2−kcoskϕ]; only its constant and third Fourier coefficients survive.

c OurBigBook.com
The square root produces branch points at z=±1, with local behaviour proportional to (z∓1)−1/2. One branch cut can join them along [−1,1]. Another choice uses the two rays (−∞,−1]∪[1,∞). Each choice prevents a loop from enclosing just one branch point within a single-valued domain. For the finite-segment choice fix z2−1​∼z at infinity. Infinity is then a pole of order three, not a branch point, since
f(z)=z3+21​z+8z3​+O(z−3).
(11)

Use the branch cut [−1,1] and the branch of a multivalued function normalized by z2−1​∼z. The Laurent series from the preceding solution has z−1 coefficient 3/8. Consequently every sufficiently large positively oriented circle gives
∮C∞​​f(z)dz=43πi​.​
(12)
Although f grows cubically, its other Laurent series terms have zero contour integral. Choosing the opposite branch of a multivalued function reverses the sign; neither the branch of a multivalued function nor the orientation can be omitted from the answer.

e OurBigBook.com
Shrink the positive outer contour to the branch cut [−1,1]. On its upper bank the chosen branch of a multivalued function has x2−1​=i1−x2​ and on the lower bank it has the negative of this value. The upper bank runs from 1 to −1, and the lower bank runs from −1 to 1. The endpoint circles contribute O(ϵ​) and vanish. Hence
43πi​=2i∫−11​1−x2​x4​dx,∫−11​1−x2​x4​dx=83π​.​
(13)
The change of variables x=sint independently reduces the result to the integral of sin4t over [−π/2,π/2].

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Kepler's third law for two point masses in a Newtonian gravitational field is
P2=G(M1​+M2​)4π2a3​.​
(14)
Here a is the semimajor axis of their relative orbit, P the orbital period and G the gravitational constant. Equivalently (P/yr)2=(a/AU)3/[(M1​+M2​)/M⊙​], to the accuracy with which these astronomical units normalize the solar mass.

b

Words: 104 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 104
b OurBigBook.com
Assume a circular orbit and an orbital inclination i≃90∘, as appropriate for a simple eclipsing binary estimate. At quadrature the two radial velocities are opposite and equal to the orbital speeds. The more massive component has the smaller amplitude. With the centre of mass as origin,
a1​=2πK1​P​,a2​=2πK2​P​,a=a1​+a2​,M2​M1​​=K1​K2​​=2.
(15)
Thus a1​=0.1103AU, a2​=0.2206AU and Kepler's third law gives
a=0.3309AU,M1​=8.06M⊙​,M2​=4.03M⊙​.​
(16)
The orbital plane contains the observer's line of sight; at quadrature the two velocities point towards and away from that observer, as labelled in the original schematic below. For an elliptic orbit, the measured amplitudes instead give asini=P(K1​+K2​)1−e2​/(2π); the numerical answer requires the circular assumption.

c

Words: 138 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 138
c OurBigBook.com
Adopt the approximate mass-luminosity relation L/L⊙​≃(M/M⊙​)3 and equal available fuel fractions. The main-sequence lifetime then scales as M/L, giving
t1​≃1.54×108yr,t2​≃6.16×108yr.​
(17)
Using an exponent 3.5 instead gives about 5.4×107 and 3.1×108 years; these are model-dependent estimates. At r=3rs​=6GM/c2 the Newtonian gravitational potential energy released from infinity is GMm/r=mc2/6. Half remains as kinetic energy in a circular orbit, so the radiatable binding energy is GMm/(2r):
ηNewtonian​=121​≃8.3%.​
(18)
Using the whole potential energy loss would give 1/6, which does not subtract the final kinetic energy. A fully relativistic calculation for a nonrotating black hole gives 1−8/9​≃5.7%. When the surviving star exhausts hydrogen burning, it expands off the main sequence and can fill its Roche lobe. Binary mass transfer to the black hole can form an accretion disk and an X-ray binary; unstable binary mass transfer may instead produce a common envelope. This is conditional on the binary star remaining bound after the first remnant forms. The supplied black hole endpoint is an assumption, not a universal outcome for an isolated 8M⊙​ star.

Solution
Words: 69
a OurBigBook.com
A thin spherical shell has outward pressure force −4πr2(dP/dr)dr and inward gravitational force GM(r)4πr2ρ(r)dr/r2. Hydrostatic equilibrium requires
drdP​=−r2GM(r)ρ(r)​,drdM​=4πr2ρ(r).​
(19)
A uniform-density solar model gives M(r)=M⊙​(r/R⊙​)3, ρˉ​=3M⊙​/(4πR⊙3​), and after integration from R⊙​ to zero,
Pc​=8πR⊙4​3GM⊙2​​=1.34×1014Pa,Tc​=ρˉ​kB​Pc​μmp​​=6.9×106K(μ=0.6).
(20)
Thus the appropriate orders of magnitude are 1014–1016Pa and 107K. The uniform-density approximation underestimates the actual central pressure because the Sun is centrally concentrated. Radiation pressure is neglected in applying the ideal gas law.

b

Words: 115 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 115
b OurBigBook.com
A free-fall timescale estimate follows from R/t2∼GM/R2:
tdyn​∼GM⊙​R⊙3​​​≃1.6×103s.​
(21)
Falling to a central point mass gives the more precise factor π/(22​), or 1.77×103s; a distributed star changes an order-one coefficient. For any spherical mass distribution with radius R,
∣Ω∣=∫0M​r(m)Gm​dm≥RG​∫0M​mdm=2RGM2​.
(22)
The inequality is strict for an extended star; equality is approached by a thin shell at R. For an monatomic gas the virial theorem is 2U+Ω=0, so half the gravitational potential energy released by contraction heats the star and half can be radiated. The Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time is therefore of order
tKH​∼2R⊙​L⊙​GM⊙2​​≃1.6×107yr.​
(23)
A uniform-density model gives 3GM2/(10RL)≃9.4×106yr. The given bound fixes a scale, rather than an exact contraction history; both estimates are far shorter than the Sun's main-sequence lifetime.

c

Words: 114 Articles: 1
2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 114
c OurBigBook.com
The right panel of the figure in solution has luminosity increasing upwards and effective temperature decreasing to the right. An old globular cluster contains a low-mass main sequence, a main-sequence turnoff, subgiants, a red giant branch, a horizontal branch, an Asymptotic giant branch and a faint hot white dwarf sequence. Its high-mass main sequence is absent because those stars have evolved.
If a fraction fc​=0.1 of the star participates in hydrogen burning, with initial hydrogen mass fraction X=0.7, the available nuclear binding energy is 0.007fc​XMc2. Assuming a roughly constant luminosity and coeval stars,
t≃1.6×1026W0.007fc​X(0.8M⊙​)c2​≃1.39×1010yr.​
(24)
Taking the quoted core fraction as hydrogen fuel itself, fc​X=0.1, gives 1.98×1010yr. Stating the fuel convention matters: burning the whole stellar mass overestimates the age by about an order of magnitude. Evolving luminosity and detailed stellar structure are needed for an accurate age.

a

Words: 129 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 129
a OurBigBook.com
The Milky Way has a thin stellar galactic disk, radius roughly 15–20kpc and scale height about 0.3kpc, containing gas, dust, young and old stars, spiral arms and most current star formation. Its stellar mass is a few 1010M⊙​. A thicker, older galactic disk has scale height around 1kpc and stellar mass of order 1010M⊙​, with little cold gas.
The central galactic bulge and bar extend a few thousand parsecs and contain about 1010M⊙​, largely older stars. The central supermassive black hole has mass about 4×106M⊙​ and is negligible in the total galactic budget. A diffuse old metal-poor stellar halo, extending tens to over 100kpc, contains globular clusters and roughly 109M⊙​ in stars. An extended dark matter halo reaches roughly 200kpc and dominates the total mass, of order 1012M⊙​. These are approximate component scales; the gaseous galactic halo also extends beyond the stellar galactic disk.

b

Words: 68 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 68
b OurBigBook.com
Treat the gravitational field as approximately spherical. The circular orbit condition gives
M(<8kpc)=Gvc2​r​=9.0×1010M⊙​,Υ=L/L⊙​M/M⊙​​=4.50.​
(25)
If every star had a representative mass m and obeyed L/L⊙​=(m/M⊙​)3, its mass-to-light ratio would be (m/M⊙​)−2, giving m≃0.47M⊙​​. This is a one-mass estimate, not an actual average inferred uniquely from the data: a galactic stellar mass function, stellar remnants, dust and nonstellar mass alter the relation. The flattening of the galactic disk also changes the spherical conversion by an order-one factor.

c OurBigBook.com
Assume an isotropic, stationary spherical galaxy cluster. Its three-dimensional velocity dispersion obeys ⟨v2⟩=3σlos2​. For a uniform sphere, the virial theorem gives 3Mσlos2​=3GM2/(5R), hence
Mdyn​≃G5Rσlos2​​=9.4×1014M⊙​.​
(26)
A different density profile changes the coefficient, so 1015M⊙​ is the meaningful scale. For isothermal X-ray gas in hydrostatic equilibrium,
M(r)=−Gμmp​kB​Tr​dlnrdlnρg​​.
(27)
Using μ=0.6 and a representative slope −dlnρg​/dlnr=2–3 at 1Mpc gives MX​≃(1.3–1.9)×1015M⊙​. The temperature and extent alone cannot fix this coefficient without a density profile. The total luminosity is 5×1012L⊙​, so the previously inferred mass-to-light ratio gives
M⋆​≃4.50(5×1012)M⊙​=2.25×1013M⊙​.​
(28)

d

Words: 60 Articles: 1
3 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 60
d OurBigBook.com
Three physically distinct contributions are unseen dark matter, hot diffuse intracluster gas omitted from the summed stellar mass, and faint stars or stellar remnants missed by transferring the Milky Way mass-to-light ratio to the cluster. The first two are actual additional components; the third changes the inferred stellar budget. Departures from virial equilibrium, velocity anisotropy or extra nonthermal pressure can also bias the dynamical or X-ray estimates, although they need not remove the discrepancy.

Solution

a OurBigBook.com
Define the canonical momentum pi​=∂L/∂q˙​i​ and the energy function E=∑i​pi​q˙​i​−L. Along an Euler-Lagrange equation solution,
dtdE​=∑i​(p˙​i​−∂qi​∂L​)q˙​i​−∂t∂L​=−∂t∂L​.
(29)
Thus an autonomous Lagrangian has conserved E. For a simple harmonic oscillator, L=mx˙2/2−kx2/2 and E=mx˙2/2+kx2/2​ is constant. For ordinary time-independent mechanical coordinates this is the total mechanical energy.

b

Words: 111 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 111
b OurBigBook.com
The appropriate invariance is invariance of the action element Ldt, including the change of the time measure. Under δt=λϕ and δqi​=λψi​, differentiation of qi′​(t′) gives δq˙​i​=λ(Dt​ψi​−q˙​i​Dt​ϕ). Therefore
λdtδ(Ldt)​=Lt​ϕ+∑i​Lqi​​ψi​+∑i​pi​(Dt​ψi​−q˙​i​Dt​ϕ)+LDt​ϕ.
(30)
Using the Euler-Lagrange equations and Dt​E=−Lt​, this becomes
Dt​[∑i​pi​ψi​−Eϕ].
(31)
An action symmetry therefore yields the Noether charge
Q=i∑​pi​ψi​+(L−i∑​pi​q˙​i​)ϕ,Dt​Q=0.​
(32)
For ϕ=0 this reduces to the usual spatial form of Noether's theorem. The same on-shell calculation permits velocity-dependent generators when they define a legitimate variational symmetry. Merely preserving the numerical value of L is insufficient for transformations of time: the Jacobian matrix and determinant dt′/dt matters. If the action changes by a boundary term λDt​B, the conserved quantity is Q−B.

c

Words: 66 Articles: 1
1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 66
c OurBigBook.com
For a central potential use L=m∣r˙∣2/2−V(∣r∣). An infinitesimal rotation about any constant unit vector n has ϕ=0 and ψ=n×r. Noether's theorem gives Q=mr˙⋅(n×r)=n⋅L, where L=r×mr˙. Since n is arbitrary, every component of angular momentum is conserved. A time-translation symmetry has ϕ=1, ψ=0, giving Q=−E and
L=r×mr˙,E=21​m∣r˙∣2+V(r)​
(33)
as conserved quantities.

After injection, the radiopharmaceutical circulates and accumulates according to its biological targeting and clearance. Technetium-99m undergoes an isomeric nuclear transition, producing approximately 140keV gamma rays; its roughly six-hour half-life permits useful counting with limited persistence. Some photons undergo absorption or Compton scattering in the patient. A lead collimator in the gamma camera accepts a narrow range of directions so the accepted event retains positional information.
An accepted gamma ray deposits energy, commonly in a NaI(Tl) scintillator, by photoelectric effect or Compton scattering. The resulting visible particle scintillation light is collected by photomultipliers. Their relative pulse sizes determine an event position and their summed pulse estimates its energy. A pulse-height analyser accepts an energy window around the photopeak to reject many scattered events. Position and uniformity corrections are applied; accepted events increment a two-dimensional pixel histogram. After acquisition the computer displays this count map as a planar projection of tracer activity. Finite counting statistics, attenuation, scattering and the collimator limit the image's quantitative accuracy and spatial resolution.[ref]

For diagnosis, an escaping gamma ray or a Positron followed by annihilation photons allows external detection, with an appropriate short half-life and limited deposited energy. For molecular radiotherapy, short-range charged emissions such as beta particles, alpha particles or Auger electrons deposit substantial local energy in the targeted tissue. Positron emission tomography uses a Positron-emitting tracer. The emitted Positron travels a short distance before electron-positron annihilation produces an approximately back-to-back photon pair. Coincident detection in a detector ring defines a line of response, giving electronic collimation and greater detection efficiency; time-of-flight PET further constrains position along that line. The positron range, non-collinearity, detector size, scatter and accidental coincidences limit spatial resolution and quantification. Start with a fast massive projectile following an approximately straight path. Its time-dependent electric field perturbs bound absorber electrons. At large impact parameter, treating the perturbation to first order and summing excitation and ionization transition probabilities gives an energy transfer weighted by the absorber's oscillator strengths. The oscillator-strength sum rule reduces the leading coefficient to the number of target electrons, while their logarithmically weighted excitation energies define I.
The classical impulse picture explains the logarithm: a transverse impulse scales as 1/(bv), so transferred energy scales as 1/(b2v2); multiplying by the number of encountered electrons in 2πbdbdx gives db/b. Quantum scattering replaces ad hoc short- and long-distance cutoffs by recoil kinematics and bound-state excitation. Relativistic projectile kinematics supplies Tmax​ and the −β2 term. Summation over many independent encounters gives the mean stopping power, rather than the energy-loss straggling of individual tracks.
The leading approximation assumes M≫me​, a sufficiently fast projectile for perturbation theory, a largely fixed projectile charge, and weak correlations between collisions. At low velocity, electron binding, charge exchange and nuclear stopping become important; at high velocity, polarization screens distant interactions and gives the density correction. The projectile's bremsstrahlung is suppressed by its large mass and is excluded from the collision stopping power.

Photon radiotherapy uses indirectly ionizing photons. Their Compton scattering, photoelectric effect and, at higher energy, pair production create charged particles that deposit energy. A megavoltage beam has a dose-build-up region followed by a gradual decline and substantial exit dose. Multiple shaped beams or intensity-modulated radiotherapy distribute this dose around a target.
Proton therapy uses directly ionizing charged particles with a finite particle range and a Bragg peak. Tuning beam energy controls depth and scanning controls lateral delivery; multiple energies cover a finite target thickness. Reduced distal and integral normal-tissue dose is a potential advantage. Limitations include range uncertainty, Multiple Coulomb scattering, nuclear secondary production, motion-dependent delivery, and a variable relative biological effectiveness, particularly near the distal edge. A physical dose advantage must be assessed against target coverage and clinically relevant toxicity; it does not by itself establish superior tumour control.

A valid comparison needs comparable disease stage, risk, systemic treatments and dose prescriptions; otherwise selection bias and confounding can masquerade as treatment benefit. Referral to specialist centres can select younger, wealthier or more complex patients. Randomized controlled trials reduce such biases but can face limited recruitment, patient preference, crossover and lack of clinical equipoise.
Both arms need expert contemporary planning and comparable quality assurance. Centre experience, changing delivery technology and an obsolete comparison arm can distort results. The chosen endpoint must match the proposed benefit: equal tumour control with lower late toxicity may be valuable even without a survival difference. Statistical power, competing mortality, multiple comparisons and long follow-up are crucial for rare late effects, particularly second cancers. Blinding of treatment delivery is difficult, so independent endpoint adjudication and predefined analyses help. Economic analyses must state their perspective and include access and follow-up costs.

The central dogma of molecular biology concerns sequence information: DNA can be copied by DNA replication; transcription makes RNA from DNA; and translation makes a protein from messenger RNA. The familiar DNA→RNA→protein diagram is not an assertion that all information transfer is one-way: reverse transcription and RNA replication are compatible with the dogma. Its key exclusion is transfer of a protein's amino-acid sequence back into nucleic-acid sequence by a general templating mechanism.
DNA is a polymer of deoxyribonucleotides with a sugar–phosphate backbone joined by phosphodiester bonds. Its usual DNA double helix contains antiparallel strands with complementary bases, adenine paired with thymine and guanine with cytosine. The base sequence stores inherited information; complementary pairing supports accurate copying and repair. A strand has distinct 5′ and 3′ ends, and ordinary chain synthesis extends the 3′ end. Packaging into chromosomes compacts and regulates access to the genetic material.
RNA uses ribose, with a 2′ hydroxyl group, and uracil in place of thymine. It is usually single-stranded but forms extensive paired secondary and tertiary structures. Messenger RNA conveys coding information, transfer RNA couples codons to amino acids, and ribosomal RNA provides both structural organization and catalysis within the ribosome. Other RNA molecules regulate expression or catalyse reactions. Thus RNA is not merely a passive intermediate.
Proteins are polypeptides of amino acids linked by peptide bonds, read from an amino terminus to a carboxyl terminus. Their primary sequence guides protein folding; backbone hydrogen bonds organize helices and sheets, while hydrophobic, electrostatic and other interactions produce tertiary and sometimes quaternary protein structure. Their functions include catalysis, transport, signalling, mechanical support and molecular movement. Sequence alone does not guarantee function: folding, modifications, partners and cellular conditions matter. During translation, a ribosome reads successive triplet codons in messenger RNA, with charged transfer RNA molecules supplying the corresponding amino acids; initiation and termination define the reading frame.

The left panel below shows paddles in a bath connected by an axle to an asymmetric toothed wheel, a spring-loaded pawl and a load. A naive argument lets random paddle kicks turn the wheel in one direction while the pawl blocks reverse motion, apparently extracting work from a single bath. The missing ingredient is the pawl's own thermal fluctuations. At the same temperature, it sometimes lifts and allows reverse slips. Correct forward and reverse transition rates obey detailed balance, so no sustained directed rotation can do work at single-bath thermal equilibrium. The device illustrates, rather than disproves, the Second law of thermodynamics.
A macroscopic shaken ratchet is driven far from thermal equilibrium: imposed shaking supplies organized mechanical energy, and friction or inelastic collisions dissipate it. Its kilogram-scale parts are not moved appreciably by molecular thermal fluctuations. Rectification requires broken spatial symmetry from the teeth or pawl and appropriate dynamical coupling: the shaking must sometimes disengage or drive the pawl over a tooth while contact and dissipation prevent equal reverse motion. The load must remain below the available mean driving torque. Isotropic, aperiodic shaking can satisfy these conditions because the asymmetric mechanism breaks directional symmetry; without the external energy supply, a working rectifier and dissipation, there is no guaranteed directed motion.

ATP synthase has a membrane-embedded Fo​ sector, a catalytic F1​ head and mechanical connections between them. The Fo​ sector contains an ion-conducting subunit a adjoining a rotating ring of c subunits. A central shaft including the γ subunit connects that ring to F1​. A peripheral stator holds the head fixed relative to the membrane. The F1​ head has three catalytic β subunits alternating with three α subunits, surrounding the asymmetric central shaft; the middle panel of solution labels these relationships.
A transmembrane proton-motive force drives proton movement through offset half-channels and protonation changes around the ring, producing torque. Shaft rotation changes the conformations of the three catalytic sites, cycling their affinities for ADP, inorganic phosphate and ATP. In the binding-change mechanism, mechanical work particularly promotes release of tightly bound ATP; the threefold head couples a full revolution to three catalytic turnovers. The number of protons per revolution depends on the ring stoichiometry. Reversing the available free energy can reverse the motor: isolated F1​ hydrolyses ATP and rotates, and the coupled enzyme can pump protons. This structural separation of rotor, stator and catalytic head converts electrochemical free energy into chemical free energy.[ref]

The Scientific Revolution is a useful name for linked transformations in European natural philosophy during roughly the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, rather than a single event with an agreed beginning or end. Its strongest scientific content is a change in how motion, the heavens and natural phenomena were represented and investigated: increasingly mathematical accounts, new instruments, controlled experiments and public argument altered what could count as a persuasive explanation. The conventional span from Nicolaus Copernicus in 1543 to Isaac Newton in 1687 captures important developments, but excludes relevant earlier work and later consolidation.
In astronomy, the heliocentric model changed the arrangement of the planets without initially discarding all older mathematical devices. Johannes Kepler's elliptic orbits and empirical Kepler's laws of planetary motion then displaced uniform circular motion as a universal premise. Telescopic observations associated with Galileo Galilei, including the phases of Venus and satellites of Jupiter, challenged specific inherited cosmological claims. Their significance depended on arguments that the telescope reliably revealed celestial phenomena, not simply on looking through an uncontroversial window.
In mechanics, idealized mathematical treatments of falling bodies and projectiles helped establish quantitative relations between motion and causes. Newton's laws of motion and Newton's law of universal gravitation linked terrestrial falling bodies with celestial orbits in a single framework. The importance of this synthesis lay in detailed quantitative problems, such as the relation between inverse-square force and planetary motion, not merely in announcing that mathematics applied to nature.[ref]
Experimental practices changed alongside theory. Air-pump work associated with Robert Boyle made carefully described apparatus, witnessed trials and replication central to disputes about air and the vacuum. Francis Bacon promoted organized inquiry, while René Descartes pursued a mathematical and mechanical account of nature; their differences caution against inventing a single timeless “scientific method”. Scientific societies, correspondence, printed diagrams and journals helped stabilize results and reputations beyond an individual's laboratory.
The term remains selective. Mathematics, craft knowledge, instruments and observations had long histories, including substantial contributions beyond Europe. Older and newer explanatory styles coexisted; natural philosophers did not suddenly become present-day professional scientists. Religious, courtly and commercial settings often supported the same work later narrated as a victory over tradition. The Scientific Revolution therefore describes a consequential reorganization of scientific questions, practices and authority, while requiring care about geographical scope, continuity and the uneven pace of change.

Doubt was reasonable if it concerned the physical cause or unlimited extrapolation of Newton's law of universal gravitation; wholesale dismissal of the quantitative evidence was harder to justify. Early eighteenth-century investigators had to distinguish the success of an inverse-square force law in explaining observations from the claim that every material body directly attracts every other one without a mediating mechanism.
The strongest case for Isaac Newton's framework was its unification of phenomena previously treated separately. Kepler's third law and nearly elliptic orbits could be connected to an inverse-square central force. Comparing terrestrial gravity with the centripetal acceleration of the Moon supported continuity between falling bodies and celestial motion. The Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica by Isaac Newton also developed treatments of interacting bodies, tides and the Earth's figure. These were substantive tests and organized a research programme capable of producing further quantitative comparisons.[ref]
There were nevertheless rational reservations. A law proportional to m1​m2​/r2 inferred from accessible bodies and distances did not logically establish unrestricted universality. Individual celestial predictions involved uncertain observations and approximations to difficult many-body classical mechanics. The Moon's motion and the Earth's shape were demanding tests whose successful treatment was not complete at the beginning of the century. A dissenter could question auxiliary assumptions, numerical accuracy or the inference from special cases without denying every success.
A deeper objection concerned explanation. In traditions requiring contact mechanisms, unexplained attraction across empty space appeared to reintroduce an occult quality. René Descartes's vortices supplied a mechanical alternative, though they faced their own serious dynamical difficulties. Newton himself separated a mathematically established pattern from a claimed cause of gravity; the 1713 General Scholium by Isaac Newton declined to invent an unsupported physical mechanism. Treating every criticism of action at a distance as a failure to understand evidence would therefore misrepresent the available positions.[ref]
Later confirmations cannot be counted as evidence already possessed by an early-eighteenth-century critic. Subsequent geodetic measurements, improved lunar theory and successful comet predictions helped shift the balance, but their timing matters. Nor did retaining a mechanical alternative remain equally reasonable after every failed prediction: responsible doubt required comparative assessment and willingness to revise it. The balanced conclusion is that selective, explicit scepticism about universality or cause was defensible, while the breadth of Newtonian mechanics' quantitative achievements already imposed a substantial explanatory burden on rival accounts.

3 OurBigBook.com
Sadi Carnot's ideal engine was deeply indebted to practical heat engines as a source of questions and physical constraints, while its decisive result depended on deliberate idealization. In 1824 steam power was an established technology, and variations in engine economy made the conversion of heat into useful work a problem with immediate industrial meaning. Comparing different working substances and operating temperatures required a theory more general than the description of one machine.
Real engines supplied the essential architecture: a working fluid, heating from a hot source, expansion producing work, cooling or condensation, and return to an initial condition. Their losses also suggested what an ideal comparison had to remove. Friction, leakage, finite temperature differences during heat exchange and incomplete expansion waste useful performance. The idea of obtaining more work by using expansion rather than simply discarding pressure connected the argument directly to engineering experience. Sadi Carnot's opening discussion explicitly places the inquiry in the context of the steam engine's practical power.[ref]
The theoretical advance was to replace those irreversible operations by a closed thermodynamic cycle. In its modern description the Carnot cycle contains an isothermal expansion at Th​, an adiabatic expansion, an isothermal compression at Tc​, and an adiabatic compression. The fluid returns to its initial state, so the result can be compared repeatedly rather than consuming a hidden initial store. Reversibility permits an engine to be run backwards and paired with another engine, providing a powerful limiting argument independent of detailed construction.
It is essential not to attribute the whole modern interpretation to 1824. Sadi Carnot reasoned within a caloric theory in which heat was conserved and motive power was associated with its passage from hot to cold, rather like a fall between levels. The modern first law of thermodynamics instead gives W=Qh​−Qc​, and the reversible entropy balance gives Qh​/Th​=Qc​/Tc​. Thus the modern result
ηrev​=1−Th​Tc​​
(57)
expresses a lasting structure of his argument in a later thermodynamic language; it should not be presented as his original derivation with contemporary concepts.
Actual engines therefore did more than decorate an abstract proof: they provided the phenomenon to explain, the operating ingredients and the direction in which improvements were sought. Yet no real engine executes a perfectly reversible Carnot cycle; finite power requires finite rates, and practical machines face material and transfer constraints. The engine is most valuable as a comparative upper limit and an argument for universality. Its historical interest lies in extracting such a general limit from engineering knowledge using an initially mistaken theory of heat, not in either pure deduction without machinery or mere generalization of workshop measurements.

Between about 1880 and 1920 a recognizable investigation of subatomic entities emerged from work on electrical discharge, radiation and atomic model. Calling it physics is retrospective: it was not yet the later high-energy specialization with accelerators, and boundaries with atomic physics, nuclear physics and chemistry remained fluid. Its formation nevertheless had both scientific and institutional causes.
Better vacuum pumps, discharge tubes, high voltages, photographic plates and sensitive electrical instruments made new phenomena experimentally reproducible. Cathode rays could be deflected by electric and magnetic fields, letting investigators compare their charge-to-mass ratio under different conditions. In 1897 Joseph John Thomson argued that their carriers were common constituents of matter with far smaller mass than an atom. This made a divisible atom an experimental research problem rather than simply a speculative possibility.[ref]
Wilhelm Röntgen's X-rays, Henri Becquerel's spontaneous uranium radiation and the work of Marie Curie and Pierre Curie on strongly radioactive substances revealed additional emissions and transformations. Their classification by penetration, charge and deflection separated physically different entities. Radioactive decay introduced characteristic lifetimes and suggested that atoms could change identity. Chemical separation and quantitative electrical measurements were therefore as important as a purely mechanical picture of particles.[ref]
Rutherford scattering made the atom's internal structure accessible to an incisive quantitative probe. Hans Geiger and Ernest Marsden measured rare large deflections, and Ernest Rutherford's 1911 analysis connected them to a concentrated nuclear charge rather than a diffuse one. The experimental task involved a collimated source, thin target foils and detection of individual scintillations at different angles; changing thickness and angle tested explanations of single versus multiple scattering. This style of inferring invisible structure from statistical distributions became characteristic of the developing field.[ref]
Specialization also depended on laboratories capable of maintaining apparatus, obtaining rare sources, training assistants and students, and circulating standardized measurements. Research schools sustained linked problems across many experiments; new journals, meetings and prizes gave their practitioners a recognizable identity. Industry supplied pumps and electrical equipment, while medical interest in radiation supplied additional demand and resources. These conditions help explain why the specialization consolidated in that period rather than emerging automatically from one discovery.
The date range should not imply completion. By 1920 the electron, nuclear electric charge, radioactivity and early nuclear transformations had established a new scale of questions, but the neutron, mature quantum mechanics and accelerator-based high-energy research still lay ahead. The emerging specialty was the joint product of experimentally identifiable new objects, a distinctive toolkit and institutions able to make their investigation a continuing career.

5

Words: 420 Articles: 1
S14 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 420
5 OurBigBook.com
Practising scientists can learn how evidence, instruments and disciplinary assumptions acquire authority, provided history is treated as a critical investigation rather than a collection of motivational stories. The useful question is not whether the past supplies a universal recipe for discovery, but which specific habits of reasoning become visible when earlier problems are reconstructed with the evidence their participants actually possessed.
First, history can discipline judgements about evidence. Early critics of Newton's law of universal gravitation faced a genuine distinction between a successful force law and an unexplained physical cause. Reconstructing that distinction discourages equating disagreement with stupidity. Conversely, the quantitative successes of Newtonian mechanics show that scepticism must answer the best available evidence, rather than invoking general uncertainty indefinitely. The transferable lesson is to separate measured regularities, modelling assumptions and causal interpretation.
Second, experiments have histories of reliability. Cathode ray measurements required vacuum control, calibrated fields and competing accounts of what a discharge tube produced. Rutherford scattering required sensitive counting, geometrical control and a statistical interpretation of rare events. These examples make instrument performance and data selection part of the argument rather than invisible background. For current practice this supports explicit calibration, reporting uncertainty, checking alternative explanations and distinguishing a missing event from a detector's failure to register it.
Third, productive models can rest on concepts later replaced. Sadi Carnot's reasoning retained an enduring reversible-engine comparison while using caloric theory. This encourages scientists to identify which conclusions depend on which premises, instead of accepting or rejecting a model as an indivisible whole. It does not mean false assumptions are harmless: their usefulness has to be established for particular questions and tested limits. Likewise an elegant idealization is not automatically a workable machine.
Fourth, the organization of work matters. Shared apparatus, trained technicians, correspondence and laboratory traditions affected which observations became possible and credible. Historical reconstruction can recover contributions obscured by a single-discoverer narrative and reveal why a method that worked in one laboratory failed elsewhere. Scientists can use that awareness to improve documentation, replication and credit without treating social context as a substitute for empirical evaluation.
There are limits. Historical episodes are not controlled experiments on “the scientific method”; selecting only successful cases produces survivorship bias, and later knowledge can make a discovery appear inevitable. Neither a slogan about revolutions nor an analogy with a famous controversy settles a present scientific dispute. Practical lessons need to be modest and specific: track assumptions, preserve evidence, inspect instruments, compare rival explanations fairly and remain alert to unrecorded work. On those terms the history of science offers intellectual tools for better scientific judgement, while leaving present claims answerable to present evidence.

The transient climate response to cumulative carbon emissions is κ≃ΔT/E​, where E is cumulative emitted carbon dioxide in a stated mass unit. These approximate compensations make warming nearly proportional to cumulative emissions; no exact cancellation follows from the logarithmic forcing law alone. a OurBigBook.com
A cold, self-gravitating region in a molecular cloud can collapse when gravity overcomes thermal, turbulent and magnetic support. Increasing central density produces a protostar, while radiation removes part of the released gravitational energy. The cloud initially carries angular momentum; material that cannot fall radially to the centre settles into a rotating protoplanetary disk. Collisions and cooling reduce random vertical motion, while angular-momentum transport allows some material to accrete and some to move outwards. Bipolar outflows and magnetic stresses can remove additional angular momentum.
The schematic sequence is rotating cloud→protostar plus disk→accreting solids and gas→planetary system plus cleared disk. In the cool disk, grains condense and collide; settling and concentration can produce planetesimals, whose gravitational growth leads to planetary embryos. Massive cores may capture gas before the disk disperses; sufficiently massive unstable disks can also form bound condensations. Migration and interactions modify the final orbits. Radiation, accretion and outflows eventually disperse the remaining gas. Thus planet formation uses the same rotating reservoir produced by ordinary star formation, although the efficiency and final architecture are not universal and individual growth stages remain active research topics.

(1−α)πRp2​σTeff4​d2R⋆2​​=4πRp2​ϵσTeq4​.

Using the supplied Bond albedos and taking the thermal emissivity ϵ=1 yields Teq,⊕​≃255K,Teq,J​≃103K​. “Perfect black bodies” must here mean perfect infrared emitters, since a perfect absorber at all wavelengths would instead have α=0, inconsistent with retaining the supplied reflected fractions. Earth's mean surface temperature of about 288K exceeds its emission temperature mainly because of the greenhouse effect. Jupiter also radiates substantial internal energy from cooling and contraction, including interior differentiation processes, so absorbed sunlight alone underpredicts its emission. Jupiter has no solid surface; the quoted 150K is a representative atmospheric level and is not identical to an effective radiating temperature.

At maximum projected separation, an Earth analogue at 10pc is separated from its star by ϑ=a/Dsys​=0.1arcsec=4.85×10−7rad. The Rayleigh criterion for a circular pupil gives
Dtel​≳ϑ1.22λ​≃1.26m(0.5μm),50.3m(20μm).​
(106)
The relevant quantity is the star–planet separation, not the tiny angular diameter of the planet itself. Simple angular optical resolution is insufficient: the planet lies in the star's diffraction pattern at reflected contrast of order 10−10, or thermal contrast of order 10−6. Residual speckles, wavefront errors, scattered light, detector/background noise and, in the infrared, strong telescope and sky thermal emission obstruct detection. A coronagraph or other stellar suppression method generally has an inner working angle of several λ/D, making practical aperture requirements larger than the bare Rayleigh criterion. The question's instrumentation claim is interpreted in its 2019 context; the physical requirements remain the basis of the estimate. Maximum reflected brightness near full phase also coincides with small projected separation, so maximum brightness and maximum resolvable separation cannot generally be obtained simultaneously.

Round-off error arises from representing numbers and carrying out arithmetic at finite precision: storing 1/3 or subtracting nearly equal numbers can lose information even when the mathematical algorithm is exact. Truncation error arises from replacing a continuous or infinite mathematical operation by a finite approximation, such as discarding higher Taylor series terms in a finite difference. Refining a grid usually reduces truncation error but may increase accumulated round-off error; the two have different origins.

ku(t+k/2)−u(t−k/2)​=ut​+24k2​uttt​+O(k4),
(107)
2D​[δxx​u(t−k/2)+δxx​u(t+k/2)]=D[uxx​+12h2​uxxxx​+8k2​uxxtt​]+O(h4+k4+h2k2).
(108)
Thus the residual, defined as left side minus right side, is
T=24k2​uttt​−8Dk2​uxxtt​−12Dh2​uxxxx​+O(h4+k4+h2k2).
(109)
Since ut​=Duxx​ implies uttt​=Duxxtt​,
T=−12k2​uttt​−12Dh2​uxxxx​+O(h4+k4+h2k2).​
(110)
This proves second-order numerical consistency in both space and time. About the old time level, uncombined Taylor remainders can include O(k3); the midpoint expression displays the symmetric leading errors most cleanly. Multiplying by k gives the one-step defect O(k3+kh2). Stable evolution with suitable initial and boundary data then gives global error O(k2+h2); consistency alone does not prove global convergence.

For balanced global error ε, a method second order in both variables can take h∼ε1/2 and k∼ε1/2. With O(1/h) work per time step in one spatial dimension, its cost scales as ε−1. A method second order in space but first order in time instead needs k∼ε, so its cost is O(ε−3/2)​ under the same per-step cost assumption. Equivalently at fixed h, using k∼h2 rather than k∼h needs about 1/h more steps. A restrictive stability condition or different linear-solver cost can dominate these accuracy-based estimates.

d OurBigBook.com
Use a smooth exact solution such as u(x,t)=e−Dq2tsin(qx) on a domain with matching boundary conditions, and compare numerical and exact values at a fixed physical time. To measure spatial order, halve h while making temporal error negligible; the error norm should fall by a factor of four. To measure temporal order, halve k on a sufficiently fine fixed spatial grid and again expect a factor of four. Report observed order p=log2​(Eh​/Eh/2​) and use several refinements to identify the asymptotic regime.
Check more than one smooth mode, boundary implementation and expected conservation or decay properties. A manufactured solution with an added known source can test nontrivial boundaries and forcing. Repeat in maximum and root-mean-square norms, stop before finite-precision or solver tolerances dominate, and separate stability failures from errors in convergence order. A single small error or a single visually smooth solution does not establish accuracy.

Let the step be h. Forward Euler method gives x1​=x0​+hv0​, v1​=v0​+hF(x0​). Applying the same map with −h gives x2​=x1​−hv1​=x0​−h2F(x0​), which generally differs from x0​. It is therefore not its own inverse under time reversal.
A kick–drift–kick leapfrog integrator instead has
v1/2​=v0​+2h​F(x0​),x1​=x0​+hv1/2​,v1​=v1/2​+2h​F(x1​).
(111)
The step −h first recovers v1/2​, then x0​, then v0​, so Φ−h​=Φh−1​​. This assumes a position-dependent force and the same fixed step. Newtonian mechanics is reversible; respecting that structure helps avoid artificial directional bias and often improves long-term qualitative behaviour. The usual leapfrog also has a structure preserving symplectic geometry, which supports bounded oscillatory energy error, but reversibility by itself does not imply exact conservation of energy. Adaptive stepping requires special care to preserve these properties.

For a second-order scalar partial differential equation, classification refers to its principal second-derivative form. An elliptic partial differential equation has a definite principal form, exemplified by Poisson's equation; it typically determines a spatial field from boundary data. A parabolic partial differential equation has a distinguished first-order evolution direction and diffusive second spatial derivatives, exemplified by ut​=Duxx​. Its initial data relax or spread with time. Thus the pseudo-time equation is parabolic, while its steady-state spatial equation is elliptic.

At a steady state in pseudo-time, ∂τ​Φ=0 and the evolution becomes Φxx​=4πGρ, the desired Poisson equation. Deviations from a steady solution obey a diffusion equation, so nonconstant error modes decay. This turns an elliptic boundary-value solve into repeated relaxation steps using familiar time-evolution methods. Boundary data and source compatibility still matter; pseudo-time does not remove a nonexistent steady solution.

AΦn+1=Φn−4πGΔτρ,A=(1+2r)I−r(S+S−1),​
(113)
where S shifts one grid cell cyclically. For J≥3, A has diagonal 1+2r, adjacent and corner entries −r, and all other entries zero. It is a cyclic tridiagonal matrix, rather than a nonperiodic tridiagonal one.
The periodic Laplacian annihilates the constant vector, so its steady equation requires j∑​ρj​=0​. A strictly positive gravitational density violates this condition: summing the update gives Φˉn+1=Φˉn−4πGΔτρˉ​, an indefinitely drifting mean. Periodic gravitational calculations normally solve for ρ−ρˉ​ and fix the arbitrary mean gravitational potential. The per-step matrix A itself remains invertible; the issue is existence of a periodic steady solution of Poisson's equation.

A numerical evolution has numerical stability if small perturbations in initial data, forcing or arithmetic are not amplified without control over the time interval of interest. For this constant-coefficient decaying linear system, an absolute-stability test requires the homogeneous numerical amplification factors to have magnitude at most one, with no growing Jordan-block contribution on the unit circle. Stability is distinct from accuracy: a strongly overdamped numerical solution can be stable while representing the physical oscillation poorly.

Words: 98 Articles: 1

Solution
Words: 98
e OurBigBook.com
An explicit numerical method normally has a simple, inexpensive step and needs no simultaneous solve, but stability can force very small steps, especially for stiff differential equations. An implicit numerical method requires a linear or nonlinear solve, storage and suitable solver tolerances; its larger stability region can permit larger steps when stability is the main restriction. Accuracy, phase fidelity and preservation of physical structure still constrain the step. For this oscillator, backward Euler method is stable but dissipative, while forward Euler method is cheap but unstable without damping. Neither statement makes all implicit methods superior to all explicit ones; method order, problem structure and total cost determine the useful choice.
